FranklinRoosevelt

Unit 5, The Great Depression and the New Deal. Part 1, 1882 to 1940

Franklin Delano Roosevelt was born in 1882 at , his family's estate on the Hudson River, and raised with a lot of money and little contact with other kids. He was an only child, taught at home and he had traveled to Europe eight times before he was fifteen, so pretty spoiled. He went to because that is where rich young men like him went.

He also grew up watching his fifth cousin become the most famous man in America, and he set out to copy Teddy’s career as closely as possible. He got into N.Y. politics young like Teddy, became like Teddy and eventually became Governor of New York you guessed it, like Teddy. In 1920 he was the Vice Presidential candidate, they lost badly but it didn’t impact his career much.

Then, at thirty nine, while on vacation, he caught and never walked unaided again. In private he used a wheelchair, in public he stood up in steel with somebody holding his arm, and moved a few yards at a time. Most Americans never knew how disabled he was. Everyone who knew him assumed his career was finished, and his mother tried to get him to retire permanently.

He would eventually return to politics, win the presidency and he stayed president longer than anyone before or since: elected four times, in office from March 1933 until he died in April 1945. He came into office in the fourth year of the , with a quarter of the country out of work and every bank shut or failing. His ‘’, permanently changed what Americans expect their government to do. Before it, they expected government to stay out of the economy. After it, they expected government to prevent disaster.

FDR was also loved and hated with unusual intensity, to most, he was a champion of the everyman, a heroic figure who, though born rich fought to help the poor. To the wealthy conservatives he was seen as a traitor to his class. There’s no doubt FDR stretched the power of the presidency to its limit. As president he signed an astonishing amount of legislation, tried to pack the , guided the country through the Great Depression and through most of World War II and ended up serving for over twelve years. Roosevelt Over the Years

Click a face. The portrait opens, and so does what the portrait was cropped to leave out.

The Hyde Park Boy 1888

He wanted for nothing, and he wanted somebody his own age to talk to.

His father was fifty four when he was born and his mother twenty six. He was their only child together. Tutors at instead of school, eight crossings to Europe before he was fifteen, and no classroom with other children until he was fourteen.

His mother, Sara, chose his clothes, his reading and his company. She was still choosing for him at twenty six, and she tried again when he was thirty nine and could not stand up.

Harvard and Eleanor 1905 to 1910

He wanted his cousin's life, and he started by marrying into it.

Franklin followed news about the way other young men followed sports. Theodore was president at the time, the most famous man in the country, and a Roosevelt. Franklin went to because that is where sons of families like his went.

In 1905 he married Eleanor Roosevelt, who was Theodore's niece. The president gave the bride away and the newspapers wrote about him instead of the couple. Franklin was Theodore's fifth cousin, which is barely related but by marrying Eleanor he truly joined Teddy’s side of the family.

FDR’s mother opposed the match and tried to stay as close to Franklin as she could.

The Navy Man 1910 to 1920

FDR tried to follow in Teddy’s footsteps as closely as possible.

He won a seat in the New York State Senate in 1910 in a Republican district, on the strength of a borrowed last name, and spent two years picking fights with , the machine that ran his own party.

is the exact job Theodore held before he became a war hero. Franklin took it at thirty one and kept it through the First World War, running shipyards and contracts and a workforce in the hundreds of thousands. When war broke out FDR asked to resign and go fight but President Wilson refused.

In 1920 his party ran him for vice president and the ticket lost badly. However, this was only a minor setback, he was thirty eight and everyone knew he would be back.

Polio 1921 to 1928

He wanted to walk again or at least be able to appear to walk again.

On holiday at , the family's summer island off the coast of Maine, he swam in cold water and woke the next morning with a fever and a weak leg. Within days he was paralysed from the chest down. He was thirty nine and the illness was .

He bought in Georgia and spent years there learning to appear upright in public using steel , a cane and a son's arm. It was an act that was difficult and painful but it allowed FDR to project able-bodiedness and the press agreed not to photograph the truth.

The water was an escape, in a pool the braces came off and he could move on his own. It is also the one place a camera could see what the braces were hiding.

Governor of New York 1928 to 1932

He wanted to prove a paralysed man could run something, and he was handed the worst economy in American history.

He was elected of New York by about twenty five thousand votes out of more than four million, which is close to a tie. Ten months later the market collapsed and the began.

New York became his proving ground. He built the first state relief agency in the country while Washington was still insisting recovery was around the corner. The photograph is what running for office looked like for him at the time.

He campaigned on crutches, in person, across a state, and four years later he campaigned across the whole country. He ran on two phrases that named no program at all: help for the forgotten man, and a new deal for the American people.

The President 1933 to 1945

He wanted the federal government to be responsible for whether ordinary people ate, and he made it so.

He took office on 4 March 1933 as the thirty second president, with every bank in the country shut or failing and roughly one worker in four out of a job. He told the crowd the only thing they had to fear was fear itself, then closed the banks himself, reopened the sound ones, and pushed fifteen major laws through Congress in a hundred days.

Right off the bat, he sat at a microphone and explained to the country what a is and why he was doing what he was doing. He gave thirty of these across twelve years; no president had ever talked to people in their own houses that way.

The did not end the Depression, and it put millions of people to work, alleviated the suffering of many Americans and transformed the country permanently.
